issues.description: The confidence scale for Experiment 1 is described in two mutually contradictory ways. The Figure 1 caption states a 4-point scale (1 = guess, 4 = certainty), while the Procedure text states a 2-point scale (1-2). This is a core dependent measure that determines which trials are classified as 'high confidence,' so the contradiction undermines interpretation of all Experiment 1 results and prevents replication.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).

issues.description: The central analytic unit is 'high confidence trials,' yet the manuscript never defines what rating(s) on the 1–4 confidence scale (Experiments 2–4) count as 'high confidence.' Without this threshold the analyses cannot be reproduced and the meaning of the reported percentages is ambiguous. The threshold also appears to differ across experiments because Experiment 1 used a different (2-point) scale.
issues.quote: After this the participant first chose the target letter from 6 different response options, and then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4).

issues.subcategory: selection bias from high exclusion rates
issues.description: Very large proportions of participants were excluded for having too few high-confidence trials (e.g., 92 of 290 in Experiment 2). Because exclusion is based on confidence behavior, and the dependent variable is itself confidence-conditioned error rates, this is a non-random selection on a variable closely related to the outcome. The included sample is systematically different (higher confidence) from the excluded sample, threatening generalizability and potentially inflating the prevalence of high-confidence illusions.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)

issues.description: Experiment 4 was run online on participants' own laptops via Zoom, yet stimulus sizes and positions are specified in degrees of visual angle (inherited from earlier lab experiments). Viewing distance, screen size, resolution, and luminance/color calibration were uncontrolled, so the intended retinal stimulus parameters could not be enforced. This undermines comparability with the lab-based experiments and the validity of timing/spatial claims.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting . Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time.

issues.description: Hypothesis 2 (memory-driven increase) in Experiment 1 is supported by averaging the 'Long' (time-based decay) and 'Short with interference' (interference-based) conditions, which are conceptually distinct manipulations with different mechanisms. Collapsing them obscures whether the increase is driven by time, by interference, or both, and the comparison baseline conditions also differ in the timing of the irrelevant display.
issues.quote: (7% increase from 19% in the short delay to 26% averaged over the short with interference and long delay)

issues.description: The transiently-induced-expectation manipulation (cue color predicting target type) produced a null effect, but the post-experiment questionnaire indicates no participant noticed the cue-target contingency. This means participants likely never learned the contingency, so the null cannot adjudicate whether transient expectations shape STM—yet the authors interpret it as evidence that expectations 'need substantial time to develop.' This conflates 'manipulation failed/unlearned' with 'transient expectations have no effect.'
issues.quote: This is consistent with the notion that expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories.

issues.description: A response-bias explanation (a general tendency to choose real letters) is dismissed as 'unlikely' purely by assertion, with no quantitative test presented to distinguish a memory-driven account from a response-bias account. Given that real letters were over-represented in Experiments 1–2, a response bias is a plausible alternative that requires direct testing rather than dismissal.
issues.quote: However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.description: In Experiment 1 the probability that the mirrored counterpart appeared as a response option differed for real vs. pseudo targets (real-target trials had the pseudo option present only ~16% of the time; pseudo-target trials had the real option present ~50% of the time). This asymmetry directly confounds the key Target Type × Error Type comparison in Experiment 1, since pseudo-to-real errors had more opportunities to occur. The authors acknowledge this and address it only in later experiments.
issues.quote: If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other 16% of the trials.

issues.description: Error rates (bounded proportions, several near floor at ~4–11%) were analyzed with repeated-measures ANOVA, which assumes approximately normal, homoscedastic data. Proportions near a floor violate these assumptions, and no transformation, generalized linear model, or check of assumptions is reported. This can distort the model comparisons that drive all conclusions.
issues.quote: The relative occurrence of illusory memories (on high confidence trials) was analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), and type of error

issues.description: The entire logic separating perceptual from memory illusions rests on the claim that 'initial perceptual inference has been completed' by the short probe (500–750 ms). However, iconic/sensory persistence and ongoing perceptual processing can extend into this window, so the 'short' condition may still tap sensory representations. The increase over time could reflect a transition from sensory persistence to reconstructive memory rather than a pure 'memory illusion,' weakening the perceptual-vs-memory dissociation.
issues.quote: If the illusions are simply the result of misperceptions, their frequency of occurrence should remain the same over the time-course of STM – since in all cases initial perceptual inference has been completed.

issues.description: All stimuli were highly overlearned alphabetic characters, yet the discussion extrapolates to visual perception/memory in general (and reinterprets prior motion-perception findings). The reinterpretation of Chalk et al. as a 'memory bias' is speculative and not tested here, and the leap to 'visual percepts in general' is not warranted by letter stimuli alone.
issues.quote: it would suggest that memory biases are not limited to letters, but instead apply to (visual) percepts in general.

issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used sequential Bayesian stopping rules with different, unjustified thresholds (BF of 6 vs. 10) and intermittent checking ('every other day'). While sequential Bayesian testing is permissible, the differing thresholds without rationale and the absence of a maximum-N or planned-stopping description raise concerns about effect-size estimation and comparability across experiments.
issues.quote: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.

issues.description: The Experiment 4 results contain a self-contradiction: a 5% difference is described as 'smaller' than a 4% difference. This makes the description of the (non-significant) three-way pattern incoherent and suggests an error in the numbers or wording.
issues.quote: There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).

issues.description: The Experiment 4 Results section refers to 'Figure 5,' but Figure 5 is the Experiment 3 figure; Experiment 4 data are in Figure 6. This mislabeling can confuse readers about which data support the reported statistics.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.description: Throughout, results are reported as point-estimate percentages and Bayes factors only, with no credible intervals, posterior effect-size estimates, per-cell trial counts, or variability around the means. This makes it impossible to gauge the precision or reliability of the reported differences (e.g., 2% vs 4% increases) and hampers meta-analytic use.
issues.quote: longer delays resulted in more illusory errors (BFincl >1000 for Memory Delay)

issues.description: Experiment 1 included a 'none of these' response option (and varied set size 6/8), whereas Experiments 2–4 eliminated it because the target was always present. Removing this option changes response strategy and the base rate of selecting any presented item, complicating direct comparison of error/illusion rates across experiments that the General Discussion nonetheless aggregates.
issues.quote: Since the target letter (and its counterpart) were always among the response options, the response option "none of these" was eliminated.

issues.description: Experiment 1 varied memory set size (6 vs 8 letters, with different numbers of pseudo-letters) but set size was not entered into the main analysis; results were 'averaged across the set size conditions.' Set size strongly affects memory load and could interact with illusion rates, so collapsing it may obscure or confound effects.
issues.quote: resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.description: After exclusions Experiment 1 retained only 23 participants for a 2×3×2 within-subjects design, while later experiments retained 59–198. The small N in the foundational experiment, combined with the confidence-based exclusion, limits the robustness of its three-way and interaction inferences.
issues.quote: resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)

issues.description: Participants received correct/incorrect feedback after every trial and were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters. Such feedback could train participants to reduce real/pseudo confusions over the session, potentially suppressing illusion rates or interacting with practice; its effect on the dependent measure is neither analyzed nor discussed.
issues.quote: They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters and received feedback on their performance after each trial.

issues.description: The manuscript does not clearly state letter case and does not address whether any mirrored letters resemble other real letters. While uppercase symmetrical letters were excluded, the possibility that some mirrored forms approximate other characters (and the lack of detail on font/case) leaves a potential stimulus confound between 'pseudo-letter' status and incidental resemblance to real letters unaddressed.
issues.quote: Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment (i.e. the symmetrical letters A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y were excluded from the memory and response displays).

issues.description: In Experiment 1 the three-way interaction has only 'anecdotal' evidence (BFincl = 2.45), yet specific quantitative patterns are interpreted from it. Drawing substantive conclusions from an interaction the data barely support risks over-reading noise.
issues.quote: Finally, there is only anecdotal evidence for a three-way interaction between Target Type, Error Type and Memory Delay (BFincl = 2.45): For pseudo-letter targets, illusory errors increase 12% as memory deteriorates

issues.subcategory: nonstandard Bayes factor labels and inconsistency
issues.description: The Bayes factor interpretation labels are idiosyncratic (e.g., labeling BF 1–3 as 'anecdotal evidence for the alternative' while elsewhere treating 0.33–1 as 'substantial evidence for the null'), and these verbal categories are applied inconsistently. Clearer, conventional reporting and consistent priors disclosure (e.g., default JZS prior settings) are needed for interpretability.
issues.quote: 1 – 3: anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis, 3 – 10: substantial evidence for the alternative hypothesis, >10: strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis

issues.description: The General Discussion states illusions were probed 'at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2),' but Experiment 1's short delay was 0.75 s (750 ms), not 500 ms. Such timing inaccuracies in the summary misrepresent the experimental parameters.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2)

issues.description: The framework treats high-confidence errors that increase over time as 'illusory memories,' but this pattern is also fully consistent with ordinary reconstructive memory and confidence miscalibration as the trace decays. The manuscript does not establish that high confidence reflects a genuine phenomenological 'memory' rather than a decision-stage bias, leaving the central construct ('STM illusion') under-validated.
issues.quote: Illusory memories should result in high confidence erroneous responses, where the participants has access to a memory trace (albeit an incorrect memory trace).

issues.description: Participant age ranges include 17-year-olds (Experiments 3 and 4), who are minors in many jurisdictions and may require parental/guardian consent. The manuscript reports only general informed consent and does not address consent procedures for minors.
issues.quote: 64 participants participated (51 women; age range 17-46 years, average age 20.5 years)
